title: Why Influential British Art Movement the Bloomsbury Group Still Matters Today
summary: British artists Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant had a 50-year relationship as friends, lovers, collaborators, and kindred creative spirits that changed the course of 20th-century art history. Now, a forthcoming exhibition, “Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury” at Tate Britain in London, offers an unprecedented deep dive into the complexities and compassion of their decades-long relationship through more than 300 artworks and hundreds of additional objects and belongings. “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event,” said Thomas Kennedy, curator of modern British art at Tate Britain, of the exhibition’s scale and depth. The artists are best known as central figures in the Bloomsbury Group, a circle of intellectuals, writers, and artists famed for their contributions to British culture as much as their unconventional lifestyles, which threw off the shackles of Victorian convention in favor of open, often tangled personal and romantic lives. Their artworks often focused on portraits and domestic scenes but embraced a flattening of form that sometimes moved into true abstraction. This is Tate’s first Bloomsbury Group exhibition in 25 years. “It’s a chance to introduce an entirely new generation of visitors to their paintings and decorative works,” said Kennedy. “The exhibition tells the story of their entire lives: the days before the Bloomsbury Group, the period during it, and their later life at Charleston, their home in East Sussex.” The group gathered at Bell’s home at 46 Gordon Square in the Bloomsbury section of London, where she lived with her sister, the author Virginia Woolf , and their brothers Thoby and Adrian Stephen. The circle came to include Bell and Woolf, their respective husbands—the art critic Clive Bell and the publisher Leonard Woolf—and Grant, along with the economist John Maynard Keynes, the novelist E.M. Forster, the painter and critic Roger Fry , and others. Bell and Grant met in 1906 and became the defining visual artists of the group. The pair worked together at Fry’s design collective, the Omega Workshops . Though Bell was married and Grant was gay, their relationship had turned romantic by 1913. In 1916, the couple moved to Charleston Farmhouse with Bell’s sons, Julian and Quentin, and Grant’s lover David “Bunny” Garnett. Bell and Grant had a daughter, Angelica, born in 1918 (though she would grow up believing Clive Bell was her father). The romantic side of Bell and Grant’s relationship eventually waned, and both took other lovers, but they remained steadfastly committed to one another for decades. The sprawling show charts the course of this nuanced relationship. Highlights include a full-scale, one-to-one reconstruction of their Charleston studio, lent by Charleston, which is currently undergoing conservation work. It also features paintings, well-known decorative objects like the Famous Women Dinner Service (50 dinner plates hand-decorated by Bell and Grant), Omega Workshops furniture, and archival photographs, sketchbooks, and letters from Tate’s collection. About 25 of the roughly 400 sexually explicit drawings Grant made in the 1940s and 1950s, found under a bed, appear in the context of his wider practice for the first time. How Bell and Grant shaped each other According to Kennedy, the driving connection between the two artists was aesthetic. “Vanessa Bell said that they spoke of nothing but art,” he said. Bell was born into a Victorian literary family, the eldest daughter of the critic Sir Leslie Stephen and older sister of Virginia Woolf. She studied at Royal Academy Schools under John Singer Sargent . Grant, meanwhile, was born in Scotland in 1885 and spent much of his early childhood in India and Burma, where his father was stationed as an army officer. Although his family intended him for an army career, he took up painting and entered the Westminster School of Art in 1902, before studying in Paris at La Palette. Art was the cornerstone of the pair’s lives and personal connection, which lasted from around 1915 until their deaths. “Their relationship was certainly unusual, but they found it deeply beneficial and fulfilling, not just in their personal lives but creatively too,” Kennedy said. In fact, as the exhibition illustrates, the couple often painted the same subject at the same time. “On shared projects the authorship of their works blends into one,” Kennedy noted. The clearest example is the Famous Women Dinner Service , which the artists made as a 1932 commission for art historian and museum director Kenneth Clark. The set represents 48 influential women, from Marie Antoinette to Pocahontas, painted in loose energetic strokes on a dinnerware set of plain white Wedgwood porcelain plates, with another two plates depicting the artists themselves. Grant is the only man in the service. “They’re working together and you can’t tell which artist is which,” he said. “So it’s a melding of their practices at certain points.” Elsewhere in the show, one sees how the two distinct artists respond to the same view. Tate owns a pair of paintings, Bell’s Still Life on a Corner of a Mantelpiece and Grant’s The Mantelpiece (both 1914) , two views of a mantelpiece which the artists painted at 46 Gordon Square, the home of the Bloomsbury Group, at the same time. Bell sat slightly to the left of Grant, who stood to her right, so each had a slightly different vantage point. The works are presented together here. For the exhibition catalogue, Tate’s paintings conservators analyzed the pigments in these similar paintings. “It seems they were using the same paints but mixing them differently on different palettes,” said Kennedy. “I think that’s a lovely nod to their relationship: they were sharing paints but creating different versions of the same scene.” The differences are as telling as the similarities. “Vanessa’s is very blocky and very Post-Impressionist ,” Kennedy said, while Grant incorporated painted collage, which he applied to the canvas and painted around. “They’re sitting in the gallery at the moment, I just put them together, and you can feel the connection.” How they made life into art at Charleston “It’s at Charleston, their creative home, where art and everyday life meld into one,” said Kennedy. “Charleston itself is a living work of art. They painted the walls and the furniture, and they included their own artworks and decorative works in the spaces. They worked on this relationship for a very long time, and as a result it’s one of the most iconic partnerships in British art history.” Bell and Grant’s understanding of the home as living work of art began at the Omega Workshops, where they both served as directors. The workshops set out to erase the line between fine and decorative art. “They wanted to expand beyond the confines of the canvas and create works on tables, chairs, fans, ceramics, any surface you could think of in the domestic space,” Kennedy said. At Charleston they carried that philosophy home. Charleston is currently undergoing essential conservation work, which made it possible for the house’s studio to travel to London as a one-to-one reconstruction. The installation makes for a remarkable viewing experience. The studio contains hundreds of objects, “everything from chaises longues to paintings and books,” according to Kennedy. “It was a creative space, where they socialized and where they raised their children,” he said. “I can’t think of a better ending to a show.” Kennedy credits Charleston’s team for the scale of the loan. “We’re very lucky to have such a brilliant team there that I can ask, ‘Can I borrow 600 works?’ and they’ll say yes,” he said. Grant’s hidden erotic world A small section of the exhibition, titled “Very Private,” explores Grant’s life as a gay man and what it meant for his relationship with Bell. Bell “was always very accepting of Duncan’s homosexuality, and she was open to him having boyfriends and other relationships,” Kennedy said. Yet the arrangement brought tension, Bell feared losing him, and Grant was sometimes jealous. Kennedy calls it “the dynamics and negotiations that need to happen in what we’d now call an open relationship.” The centerpiece is a group of about 25 drawings selected from roughly 400 that Grant made in the 1940s and 1950s. The sexually explicit nudes feature a diversity of homosexual encounters. Whether they’re based in reality or fantasy remains a mystery. Grant gave the drawings to his friend, the painter Edward Le Bas, who kept them secret and safe for some 60 to 70 years. They were recently found under a bed and are now in Charleston’s collection. The Tate’s show is their largest public outing yet. The works, and their rare survival, speak to the culture of the era. “At the time, homosexual acts between men were illegal in the U.K.,” Kennedy explained. Within the Bloomsbury Group, “you could love who you wanted,” but “society as a whole did not accept Duncan, and he felt he had to hide part of himself in public. So these are an escape for him in some ways.” Kennedy has placed the drawings alongside Grant’s public work, including Bathing (1911), a mural-scale commission of nude men diving into the Serpentine. The curator believes it’s the first time the drawings have been shown in the context of the artist’s larger practice. For Kennedy, their survival is both remarkable and poingant. “I think it’s an extraordinary record of queer history that they’ve been found again,” he said. “So much of that has been destroyed over the years. We’re very fortunate that they were kept safe by these friends and lovers and passed down through the queer community.” The lasting influence of their legacy Kennedy says the show also aims to correct the record of Bell and Grant’s personal lives. “Some of the tales around the Bloomsbury Group have been blown out of proportion,” he said. “In this show we wanted to bring things down to earth and tell the story of their very loving relationship and what it meant for their art.” Chief among the misconceptions is that the partnership was inauthentic. “I think some people think there wasn’t love there, or that it wasn’t real,” Kennedy said. The letters in Tate’s archive suggest otherwise. “They could have been with other people if they’d wanted to, but they made a commitment to be with one another, even if it was unconventional.” Their artistic influence is equally underappreciated. Kennedy notes that Bell and Grant created some of the first abstract works in Britain, “which is little discussed about their practices,” and that they were “creating something unexpected and new, against the grain of the British establishment at the time.” The exhibition includes several of these paintings and drawings. Their example still resonates with working artists. The catalogue includes responses from artist couples, among them the New Zealand artist Francis Upritchard and her husband, the designer Martino Gamper , who wrote about the Omega Workshops. After learning about Bell and Grant’s work, Kennedy said, they felt compelled to paint their own cupboard doors. “It’s about pushing aside expectation and tradition and doing something creative in your own home,” they shared. For Kennedy, that is the larger lesson the artists still embody. “It’s them exemplifying another way of living, with their friends and family,” he said. “They all did it together, a tight-knit group outside mainstream British society and its expectations, creating art and literature the way they wanted to.”

title: Balenciaga marks 25th anniversary of Le City bag with Damien Hirst collaboration.
summary: Balenciaga is marking the 25th anniversary of its Le City bag, launched in 2001, with a limited-edition collaboration with artist Damien Hirst . The series introduces an original pattern drawn from two of Hirst's most recognizable motifs—his perfectly round, multicolored spots, here arranged into the simplified shape of a butterfly—applied across the bag's relaxed silhouette and classic hardware. Other pieces in the collaboration extend further into Hirst's visual vocabulary, with mandalas built from metamorphosed wings, embroidered patches distilling his best-known works and titles, and his “Spin Paintings” rendered across the bag. The series spans the Le City bag's mini, small, medium, and large sizes, along with wallets, pouches, card holders, and micro bag charms. Each is marked with a hand-lettered portmanteau of the two names, Damienciaga. Designed by Nicolas Ghesquière, Le City launched in 2001 as a deliberate counterpoint to the structured, logo-driven handbags that dominated the era, drawing on the motorcycle jacket with its use of lambskin, buckles, and whipstitched handles. An early prototype caught the eye of Kate Moss , whose enthusiasm is credited with helping push the bag into production. It went on to become a fixture among figures including Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen, Nicole Richie, Gisele Bündchen, and Sarah Jessica Parker, earning it the nickname the "Anti-It Bag" from the fashion press. The silhouette has since been reworked several times, including through Demna's Neo City in 2020 and Le Cagole in 2022. In 2024, the original design returned and received a more luxurious runway treatment in 2025 under Pierpaolo Piccioli 's debut Balenciaga collection. Alongside the Hirst collaboration, Balenciaga has launched a two-chapter anniversary campaign featuring Isabelle Huppert, Nicole Richie, Rachel Sennott, footballer Hugo Ekitike, and actor-singer Cecilia Boey, each reflecting on their own relationship with the bag. The anniversary also includes Le City House, a series of immersive installations opening at Balenciaga's historic Paris address on Avenue George V through November 19th, featuring archival designs, photographs, and personalization services including handle re-lacing and custom monogramming, before traveling to New York, Tokyo, Shanghai, and Beijing.

title: The 5 Best Booths at West Bund Art & Design 2026
summary: The opening day of this year’s Shanghai Art Week coincided with a sharp drop in temperature and a slight dip in international foot traffic compared to previous years. This is perhaps a natural shift given the absence of the local biennial and a packed autumn circuit in Japan (spanning Art Week Tokyo and Art Collaboration Kyoto ). Still, Shanghai’s creative momentum shows no signs of slowing down. Shanghai’s Art Week is among the most vibrant and bustling of any art capital globally—and it continues to grow. Instead of remaining confined to central art hubs in the city, pop-up exhibitions, satellite fairs, and cross-over initiatives spilled outward into luxury resorts and suburban sites. This citywide dispersion mirrors the growth of West Bund Art & Design , which is returning for its 12th edition this week. “It’s great to see how Shanghai Art Week has continued to develop into a well-coordinated, city-wide event, and this shows in the attendance and enthusiasm we’ve felt during the opening day of the fair,” said Dawn Zhu, director, Asia, at Thaddaeus Ropac . Ropac reported key sales within hours of the doors opening, including new paintings by Megan Rooney , which sold for £400,000 ($533,060) to a private foundation in China, and a work by Martha Jungwirth , which sold for €220,000 ($245,087). “With the size of the collector base in China, even if the current economy worsens, you can still easily find 100 new collectors capable of buying works above the half-million-dollar mark,” noted JJ, a Shanghai-based collector who recently inaugurated his own collection space. He believes that while international interest in the Chinese market has softened in recent years, the sheer scale of China’s domestic market continues to sustain commercial momentum. Here, we share five standout booths from West Bund Art & Design 2026. White Cube Booth 1C05 With works by Tunji Adeniyi-Jones, Georg Baselitz, Damien Hirst, Shigeo Otake, Tesfaye Urgessa, Liu Wei, Sarah Morris, Darren Almond, Minoru Nomata. Prominent works from the leading artists were on full display at White Cube’s standout booth, anchored by Georg Baselitz ’s over-three-meter-tall golden painting, Das zweite Mal Großgold . Created in 2025, the monumental canvas belongs to the final body of work produced during the late master’s lifetime. Flanking Baselitz’s piece was a new Damien Hirst painting, Blood Life (2026)—freshly retrieved from the artist’s studio and echoing anticipation for his upcoming exhibition at the Museum of Art Pudong in Shanghai at the end of the year. title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Xolo Cuintle
summary: Concrete is everywhere in our cities, but in the hands of Paris-based artist duo Xolo Cuintle , it becomes almost unrecognizable. Working the industrial material by hand, much like clay, Romy Texier and Valentin Vie Binet create sculptures that seem at once petrified and alive. “It’s not really us who control the material, but sometimes we feel like the concrete is controlling us,” they told us. The duo, who have worked together since 2020, take their name from the xoloitzcuintle , a hairless dog associated with the passage between life and death in Aztec mythology. “We’re very interested in creating strangeness in familiar objects,” they explained. “Is it a chair? Is it a plant? Is it a sculpture? We like this idea that things are not one thing or the other. They are not black or white; they are gray.” Dust to Dust, 2023 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie First Knot, 2026 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie Each project begins with a “script,” often inspired by the site where the work will be shown. For research, the duo frequents the Bibliothèque de l’Institut national d’histoire de l’art (INHA) in Paris, where they amass visual references before returning to the studio to experiment with concrete and incorporate cast plants into their sculptures. Xolo Cuintle is represented by DS Galerie in Paris. Their sculptures are held in the collections of the Centre national des arts plastiques and the Fonds régional d’art contemporain Île-de-France, and they’ve completed public commissions in Paris, including a sculpture garden in the 18th arrondissement and a bas-relief façade at Square du Temple. Bulb Study of a Arum Psychoda, 2024 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie Buried Seed Crossroad, 2025 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie Named 2026 “Oui Design!” laureates by Villa Albertine, they currently have a solo exhibition, “O Horizon,” at Mécènes du Sud in Montpellier, France, on view through December 19th. They also recently completed a public commission for the 2026 Jing’an International Sculpture Project in Shanghai, curated by UCCA Lab. We caught up with Xolo Cuintle in Paris, at the INHA library and in their studio in Aubervilliers, France. Watch the video above and explore The Artsy Vanguard 2027 . Heart Shaped Couple, 2021 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie Video credits: Executive producer: Casey Lesser Creative director: Molly Gottschalk Director/DP: Matteo Lonardi Editor: Jack Kuczala Designer: Douglas Escalante About The Artsy Vanguard Now in its ninth year, The Artsy Vanguard is our annual celebration of 10 of the most promising artists working today. Spanning painting, sculpture, ceramics, photography, and more, the 2027 cohort brings together a new generation of artists making work that feels fresh, urgent, and distinctly their own. Through an original 10-part video series, we visit each artist in their studio and city, offering an intimate look at their creative processes, inspirations, and what it means to be an emerging artist today. Together, these are the talents shaping what’s next in contemporary art.

title: Louis Vuitton shoots Cruise 2027 campaign at New York's Frick Collection.
summary: The backdrop for Louis Vuitton ’s Women's Cruise 2027 campaign is a Gilded Age icon. The campaign was shot inside The Frick Collection in New York. Photographed by Ethan James Green , the campaign stars house ambassadors, actor Chase Infiniti and figure skater Alysa Liu alongside actors Giulia Maenza and Amiah Miller. The models are pictured throughout the Frick's historic galleries, libraries, and salons, posing and even lounging in front of masterpieces of the museum’s collection. Works by James Abbott McNeil Whistler and Jacques-Louis David were among those spotted in the campaign imagery. “The Cruise collections have always been about movement, emotion, and the encounter between silhouettes and place,” said Nicolas Ghesquière, artistic director of Louis Vuitton's women's collections. “For the Cruise 2027 campaign, I wanted to extend that dialogue through a tale of two cities—between Paris and New York, expressing legacy and modernity. The campaign reflects the layered identities, contradictions, and cultural energy at the heart of the collection, where each look becomes part of a conversation between history, colorful expression, and imagination.” The campaign sets sharply tailored, modern silhouettes against the Frick's Gilded Age interiors and plays off the museum's gilded frames and wood-paneled rooms. In one shot, Liu is shown wearing a textured leather wrap jacket with Art Deco detailing. Infiniti appears in metallic Licorice Sneaker boots and a floral, balloon-sleeved dress in another. Accessories punctuating the looks include the new Highline bag, a colorful soft Speedy 30, the Multipass in beige, and the house's Side Trunk handbag. The campaign shoot is the latest in an ongoing three-year partnership between the Frick and Louis Vuitton. This past May, the museum hosted its Cruise 2027 runway show , which paid tribute to the artist Keith Haring . The Louis Vuitton Cruise 2027 campaign launched on November 5th and will roll out across Louis Vuitton's digital channels on November 13th, the same day the collection becomes available in Louis Vuitton stores and on louisvuitton.com.

title: Jenna Gribbon’s Paintings of Her Wife Capture the Messy Boundaries of Intimate Relationships
summary: When I meet the artist Jenna Gribbon , there is a painting of a blue-skinned, many-armed woman with a third, impossibly bright pink nipple at the center of her chest. At the center of the canvas is a recognizable figure for those familiar with Gribbon’s work: her wife, the musician Mackenzie Scott. Her form is overlaid with projections of Gribbon’s own naked body so that the two women appear fused together, resembling Kali, the Hindu goddess for whom the painting is named, the Divine Mother who presides over time, death, destruction, and transformation. Gribbon has devotedly painted her wife for close to a decade, making her the central figure in exhibitions including her 2023 exhibition “The Honeymoon Show!” at Levy Gorvy Dayan. Now, in a new show at David Kordansky in New York, the artist shows her in a whole new way, no longer simply a muse but as a seemingly mythic being with whom Gribbon is entwined. It’s Kordansky’s first New York presentation of her work, on view through December 19th, and in it Gribbon reckons with the complexity and intimacy of perceiving those we are closest to. Though the artist has spent years painting her wife, she knows truly seeing and observing someone in the moment rather than working off of our ingrained assumptions can be tricky work. In Gribbon’s estimation, a person can be different between breakfast and lunch. “There is the challenge of really seeing someone you’re intimate with. The closer you become, the harder it is to see them,” said Gribbon. “One of the greatest obstacles in seeing someone is not projecting yourself onto them. I’m literally doing that in this painting, though, showing what that reality feels like: trying to see someone but getting in your own way and seeing yourself instead.” For the large-scale works in the exhibition, Gribbon used a film projector to superimpose photographs of her own body onto Scott’s, so that the resulting figures are both mythical and monstrous. A third eye opens on a torso in one painting, a two-headed woman appears in another. The projector has its own distinct effects on these images, casting blue tones and bands of color across their chimerical forms. The exhibition juxtaposes these larger-than-life paintings with a series of small-scale paintings in warm, natural tones. These paintings offer snapshots of the artist’s domestic life—a kitchen table, a small self-portrait. In some ways, these images continue Gribbon’s practice: Scott has served as a muse and model for the artist for years. But now, Gribbon inserts herself into the picture, complicating her role as artist and viewer. The overt sensuality of Gribbon’s earlier work transmutes into something cooler and more cinematic. How Gribbon paints two portraits as one These aren’t the first merged figures that Gribbon has painted. For her 2024 exhibition “Like Looking in a Mirror” at David Kordansky in Los Angeles, Gribbon painted a series of works fusing her likeness with that of her son. “It was this time in his life where he really looked like my twin,” said Gribbon. “It was this stage before his face masculinized. We had the same hair at the time, too. It was kind of crazy.” In these paintings, Gribbon felt she was sorting out the boundaries between herself and her child. “I was projecting myself onto him to address the difficulty of parsing out where I end and he begins: what’s his and what’s mine, what’s learned, what’s inherited,” she said. Her use of the projector came earlier. In a 2021 show at Sim Smith in London, Gribbon screened the films of Agnès Varda , letting the light of the films fall across the audience. Gribbon’s first projector-based paintings of Scott came recently, in the lead-up to her museum exhibition “Entwined,” Gribbon’s first solo museum exhibition, at the Rose Art Museum, on view through January 3rd. Three new works in the exhibition show Gribbon’s own face projected onto her wife’s. To make these works, Gribbon first photographs herself, sometimes in front of a bright color. Gribbon projects those photographs onto Scott as she stands before another color. Gribbon then paints from a photograph of those two merged images. For Gribbon, this multistep process has opened her to new compositional possibilities. “That fracturing of the image and the color arrangement is a really fun painterly tool,” she said. Lesbian merging and myths This merging of forms is, in some sense, one of Gribbon’s biggest fears. “There’s this idea of lesbian merging that has always been so scary to me,” said Gribbon. “It’s a trope that lesbians become one unit and lose their individual identity, becoming extremely enmeshed.” For Gribbon, a fiercely independent person, the idea felt frightening. In these works, she dives headlong into that anxiety and considers it from other angles. “What if we combine into something powerful or mythical? What if we get superpowers?” she said. Here, these fused forms appear like Janus, the Roman god of transitions, “a single entity that looks forward and backward,” in her words, or the many-breasted Artemis of Ephesus in another. “Maybe in the combination, we can become greater than the sum of our parts,” she said of their combined forms. “We can combine into something more extraordinary or more interesting or more powerful than we have the ability to be on our own. She has so many strengths that I don’t have. And so in being partnered with her, I get to benefit from those strengths and she gets to benefit from my strengths.” Viewers, Gribbon knows, often fixate on the nudity and sensuality in her works. “People get distracted by the pink nipples,” she said. Gribbon describes the images as being as much about romance as they are about perception. “They’re about asking questions about how we’re looking, how we’re given permission to look, how we’re supposed to look versus how we want to look,” she said. The small paintings are more mundane in tone than the larger paintings, turning monsters back into familiar faces. The exhibition includes a rare small-scale self-portrait, painted from a mirror, which Gribbon describes as a moment of the couple “uncombining.” The painting showed Gribbon her own blind spot. “I feel like I’m painting a different person every time I make a painting of Mackenzie,” she said of Scott. But painting herself becomes something more complicated: “I can’t see my own evolution.” Her influences Throughout her career, Gribbon has bridged art historical influence, from Jean-Honoré Fragonard to Édouard Manet and Mary Cassatt , with contemporary figuration and cinema. For these works, she says she was thinking of French painter and writer Francis Picabia ’s “Transparencies,” the layered, overlapping paintings he made in the late 1920s and early ’30s. Gribbon admires the irreverence and playfulness of these images as well as their strangeness. This Surrealist impulse factors into how Gribbon imagines Scott, too. “I always kind of think of her as like Alice in Wonderland , like growing and shrinking. It’s like she drinks the tea and then she’s in the small painting and we’re back in our home, and then she eats the cookie and she grows into this like mythic beast,” she said. There are other art-historical narratives hidden in Gribbon’s paintings: for example, she often paints Scott wearing a pearl earring, a nod to Vermeer ’s Girl with a Pearl Earring (ca. 1665). For Gribbon, these ever-evolving stories are all just new ways of seeing Scott. “Dedicating yourself to really seeing your partner is a very romantic thing to do,” she said. “But it’s also a time-based project about the way that we evolve as people. We are all sort of changing all the time, both inside and out.”

title: Japanese Artist Mariko Mori Is Creating Hopeful Artworks for the AI Age
summary: A photograph shows a silver alien standing in an office, proffering tea to disinterested men in suits. Several rooms away, an iridescent, teardrop-shaped spaceship is moored, luring onlookers up its pearlescent pebble-steps. Meanwhile, in the next room, an obelisk of human height behind a silk veil glints blue and purple in the sun. These disparate visions are all artworks by Japanese artist Mariko Mori from the past three decades, on view as part of the artist’s retrospective “All That Shines” at the Mori Art Museum, Tokyo, through March 28, 2027. In Mori’s light, shimmery world, everyone and everything is linked, bringing all of humanity, nature, and technology together. It’s a balm for the current global climate, where divisions in society, and strife between nature and human-made tech are rampant. Mori’s works invite the viewer to put aside differences to remember that we are all connected. Mori grew up in Tokyo and was close to art from a young age, accompanying her art historian mother on sabbaticals. When she was about nine, she happened upon a Jackson Pollock postcard. “It was like freedom,” she remembered in an interview, “but I was more focusing on fashion when I was in high school, not in art.” She began modeling from the age of 16 and studied fashion design at Bunka Fashion College, before moving to London to study fashion when she was 22. But she’d enrolled in an art course by accident and called her mother, who advised her to stick it out for a year. It was in London that she first came across installation art, which completely changed the way she thought about the subject—it reminded her of how she played in childhood. “It’s total freedom to do however you like to construct within a space,” she said, drawn to the spatial element of the medium. Mori began her artistic career working with photography, using the lens of anime and otaku culture to call out dated gender roles in Japanese society by inserting herself into the narrative. In Tea Ceremony I (1994), she dressed as an alien to serve tea to passersby in a busy Tokyo district. In another work, Play With Me (1994), she documented a performance where she wore a blue wig and stood outside a Japanese store selling game and anime-related merchandise. Yet, the longer she lived away from Japan, the more her appreciation grew for the country that raised her. She moved to New York, where she encountered a wide range of diversity. “[I felt that] you have to be an ambassador of your own culture,” she said. “Finding my own identity was really necessary.” As a result, she started to design and wear anime-style clothes to parties, and to practice traditional tea ceremonies (which she still does today). But in 1996, something shifted. She had begun pondering the death of her father, a professor specialising in economics and engineering, who had died at the start of the decade (his brother also built the Mori Art Museum). She wondered “Where did he go? Or what happened to his spirit? Or is it life and it’s all finished?” Searching for answers, she began to read Buddhist philosophy and visit monks, which led her to create Enlightenment Capsule (1996–98), a glass “meditation pod.” In that work, she used her father’s invention: the Himawari system, which filters sunlight through fiber optic cable. Within the capsule, this system relays ever-changing rainbow hues. In her photographic series, “Esoteric Cosmos,” from the same period, she’s depicted as a Buddhist priestess, joined by floating, unidentifiable characters playing traditional Japanese instruments. By some readings, it’s a vision of what happens after we die. In her retrospective, the clearest throughline is Mori’s focus on the afterlife. “I just continued to search, and…I think this exhibition shows my journey,” she said. What began as a way to process grief has more recently changed into something more positive. The majority of her newer works are made in pastel and pearlescent hues, reflecting this lighter subject matter in a literal way. She worked with structural engineers and software developers to create Dream Temple (1997–99), a work that was inspired by the Temple of Dreams in Horu-ji Buddhist temple in Nara, Japan. As she looked through her works in preparation for the retrospective, she explained how she can see that her grief changed into love. “When I look through all this work, I found so much love—a lot of my work requires many collaborators and so much effort and craftsmanship and engineering.” For example, to create Tom Na H-iu (2006), a three-meter-high frosted glass plinth that was inspired by the Stones of Stenness in Scotland, she worked with Super-K neutrino observatory in Japan, a glass workshop in Padua, Italy, and an Italian production studio. The light inside reacts to a subatomic particle recorder in Japan. Mori’s creations all hint at another aspect of her undying inspiration. Since 2003, she has worked in front of the sea, and built Yuputira , her studio and an artwork itself, in front of the ocean, in 2022. It’s here where she draws and paints her “Unity Drawing” series, of iridescent paper works of divine circles and vertical lines. Her desk looks out over Miyako Bay, where she ponders the connection between humanity and nature.“[Drawing is my] fundamental practice to feel the nature quality within ourself,” she said. In 2010, Mori also founded the Faou Foundation, which works to install her artworks in nature. To date, she has permanently installed her art by a waterfall in Rio de Janeiro and on Miyako Island, near her studio. According to retrospective co-curator, Alexandra Munro, whose company is a donor to the foundation, Mori hopes to place one of her works in a UNESCO-registered site in Ethiopia. Considering her love of nature, Mori’s approach to AI may seem surprising to some. She has created artwork with the help of AI, and sees it as a source of hope for the future. “[Using AI] should be a joyful thing, an extension of our being,” she said. Whatever tool you use, she said, visualizing our reality is up to how we feel inside. “When you have hope, you project hope.” Mori’s bubble-wrapped world, where humanity, science, religion, and nature work in harmony, is drawn with a range of tools, including her pearly silver pen.

title: Do Ho Suh’s first New York museum survey to open at the Guggenheim in February 2027
summary: The Guggenheim Museum in New York will present the first major museum exhibition in the city dedicated to Korean artist Do Ho Suh , opening in February 2027. Titled “I dream in another language,” the survey will span more than three decades of the Seoul-born artist’s practice and comprise over 50 works—drawings, sculptures, and large-scale installations—that explore how we move through and carry the spaces we inhabit. The exhibition will mark the world premiere of Rubbing/Loving: Apartment A and B, 348 West 22nd Street, New York, NY 10011, USA (2014–26), a walk-through installation that reconstructs at full scale the two Chelsea apartments Suh occupied for nearly 20 years. Working across multiple years, Suh covered the interiors of both units with paper before rubbing their surfaces with pastel and colored pencil, transferring the texture and memory of the rooms into the work itself. “It is a love letter to New York,” said Kyung An, curator of the Asian Art Initiative at the Guggenheim, who organized the exhibition. Suh is best known for a body of work that treats architecture as a key element in lived experience, his works referencing memory, longing, and loss. Having moved from South Korea to the United States in his late twenties, he has spent much of his career working through what it means to inhabit multiple places simultaneously, never fully belonging to any one of them. His signature fabric installations, often full-scale reproductions of apartments, corridors, and staircases created from translucent polyester, contain specific details yet give the impression of being weightless. That preoccupation with threshold and transit has made Suh one of the most important artists working today. Hub-1, Entrance, 260-7, Sungbook-Dong, Sungboo-Ku, Seoul, Korea, 2018 Do Ho Suh Lehmann Maupin Other highlights in the Guggenheim include Some/One (2004), an imposing robe constructed from military dog tags; Hubs (2011–), an ongoing series of translucent fabric passageways drawn from the corridors and entrances of the artist’s former homes and studios; and works from Fatherhood (2011–), an ongoing series examining how memory is transmitted across generations. Throughout the four galleries, works on paper will demonstrate Suh’s distinctive technique of embedding stitched lines into wet paper pulp. Suh studied at Seoul National University before moving to the United States in 1991, earning his BFA at Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) and his MFA at Yale. His work is held by institutions including the Museum of Modern Art , the Whitney Museum of American Art , Tate, and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art . Recent solo exhibitions have been staged at Tate Modern in 2025 and MMCA Seoul in 2026. He is represented by Lehmann Maupin and Victoria Miro .

title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Maddy Inez
summary: “My grandfather was a ceramicist, but ancestrally, all humans have a relationship to clay,” Maddy Inez told us. For the Los Angeles–based artist, clay offers a way to explore the connections between people, plants, and history. Before beginning a sculpture, Inez looks at plants through a microscope and studies botanical illustrations. “I will take each part of a plant and assemble it into a type of being or humanoid form,” she explained. “I would describe it as votives of the spirits of plants.” She builds the vessels by hand, with coils of clay, and mixes her own glazes, leaving the final results, in part, up to the kiln. Okra Weaver, 2025 Maddy Inez Megan Mulrooney Benne Blessing, 2026 Maddy Inez Megan Mulrooney Inez’s recent work explores the histories of plants carried across continents through enslavement and displacement, from okra to black-eyed peas. “I started interviewing gardeners in Los Angeles—land stewards, herbalists, and educators—and asking them their idea of revolution and land and working with land,” she said. “And from their answers, I started making the new pieces.” Art runs in her family. Her mother is Alison Saar , her brother, Kyle Leeser, is also an artist, and her grandmother was the late pioneering assemblage artist Betye Saar . “My grandmother, Betye Saar, taught me before I could speak the importance of the language of art,” she recalled. Scorpion Weed, 2025 Maddy Inez Megan Mulrooney Fevered Fledgling, 2025 Maddy Inez Megan Mulrooney Inez is represented by Megan Mulrooney , where she presented her solo exhibition “ Nascence ” this spring, featuring ceramic vessels and wall works. Her work has also appeared at EXPO Chicago and Felix Art Fair, and she is slated for a solo booth with the gallery at Frieze Los Angeles in 2027. We caught up with Inez in Los Angeles, where she welcomed us into her studio, introduced us to Rojo, the tortoise she inherited from her grandmother, and took us along on her daily commute to the studio, along with her chihuahua, Ickis. Watch the video above and explore The Artsy Vanguard 2027 . Tip Toe, 2023 Maddy Inez Megan Mulrooney Pythia Pollen, 2023 Maddy Inez Megan Mulrooney Video credits Executive producer: Casey Lesser Creative director: Molly Gottschalk Director/DP: Maya Fuhr Editor: Jack Kuczala Designer: Douglas Escalante Production company: Institute Artist About The Artsy Vanguard Now in its ninth year, The Artsy Vanguard is our annual celebration of 10 of the most promising artists working today. Spanning painting, sculpture, ceramics, photography, and more, the 2027 cohort brings together a new generation of artists making work that feels fresh, urgent, and distinctly their own. Through an original 10-part video series, we visit each artist in their studio and city, offering an intimate look at their creative processes, inspirations, and what it means to be an emerging artist today. Together, these are the talents shaping what’s next in contemporary art.

title: Artist Vija Celmins and director Denis Villeneuve honored at star-studded LACMA Art+Film Gala.
summary: The Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) hosted its 15th annual Art+Film Gala on November 7, honoring artist Vija Celmins and filmmaker Denis Villeneuve. The event, co-chaired by LACMA trustee Eva Chow and Leonardo DiCaprio, welcomed more than 600 guests and raised nearly $7 million, a record for the event. These funds will go towards the museum’s film initiatives and broader programming. The evening featured a performance by musical guest ROSÉ, including the live debut of her new single “New Trick.” “It was a privilege to recognize the extraordinary careers of Vija Celmins and Denis Villeneuve, whose work can alter our perception of the visual world or transport us to worlds of the imagination,” said Michael Govan , director of the museum. Celmins, accepting her honor, reflected on how Los Angeles shaped her meticulous renderings of oceans, deserts, and night skies. “Los Angeles had a big influence on me. I had never lived next to the ocean, and I had never seen the land, and it sort of crept into my work,” she recalled. Villeneuve, introduced by Nicole Kidman, said, “When a museum, a temple for artists, welcomes a filmmaker and puts the spotlight on cinema, it means a great deal to me. Especially this museum, because LACMA has already given me so much.” Chow, who has co-chaired the gala for all 15 of its editions, used the evening to announce that this would be her final year in the role. “Seeing the gala become one of Los Angeles’s most celebrated traditions has been one of the great privileges of my life,” she said. “I leave this chapter with tremendous pride, and above all, gratitude. I hope the gala will continue to grow and inspire future generations, bringing together the world of art and film for many years to come.” Govan paid tribute to Chow ahead of the announcement, crediting her with bringing together “so many artists, filmmakers, designers, and creatives.” Guests arrived against the backdrop of Chris Burden ’s Urban Light (2008)—the museum’s iconic outdoor installation of a forest of streetlights—for a cocktail reception before dinner overlooking Michael Heizer ’s Levitated Mass (2012). Govan also used the evening to announce the installation of Shio Kusaka ’s Beam , a new public sculpture on the museum’s terrace, made possible by the trustees’ support. Artists in attendance included Ed Ruscha , Catherine Opie , Jacqueline Humphries , Kenny Scharf , Mickalene Thomas , Lauren Halsey , Refik Anadol , and Christina Quarles . Other celebrities at the event included Timothée Chalamet, Kim Kardashian, Viola Davis, Andrew Garfield, Salma Hayek Pinault, Olivia Munn, Al Pacino, Sarah Paulson, Anya Taylor-Joy, Emma Watson, and Paris Hilton, among hundreds of others from film, fashion, and music. The red carpet brought its own share of standout fashion, with Gucci —the night’s presenting sponsor—turning out custom looks for model Alex Consani, in a sculptural black gown; model and musician Soo Joo Park, in a feathered dress; and writer and curator Antwaun Sargent, in an intricately detailed ensemble. Kylie Jenner wore a brown-and-silver deer-print gown from Ashi Studio’s spring/summer 2026 couture collection, while ROSÉ performed in custom Saint Laurent .

title: Indian artist Arpita Singh dies at 89
summary: Arpita Singh , the modernist painter whose dense, densely populated canvases traced the inner and political lives of Indian women across six decades, died Monday at Fortis Hospital in New Delhi. She was 89. Her husband, the artist Paramjit Singh , told the Press Trust of India the cause was an age-related ailment. “She had heart and lung-related issues for some years now,” Paramjit said. “However, she was actively working. Her health dipped in the last three days, and she was admitted to the hospital.” Singh was born in 1937 in Baranagar, in what is now West Bengal in India. She grew up amid India’s struggle for independence and the violent 1947 partition, themes that would recur throughout her work. Later, major national inflection points, including the 1975 state of emergency and the economic liberalization of the 1990s, also shaped her worldview. She went to art school on the advice of her high school principal, earning a diploma in fine arts from Delhi Polytechnic in 1959. She went on to work as a textile designer at the Weavers' Service Centre, a postwar government institution that shaped the early careers of numerous Indian modernists. There, she absorbed the narrative folk traditions, including pattachitra scroll painting and kantha embroidery, which would become lifelong influences alongside Bengali poetry and Western Surrealism . She began painting and, in the 1960s, emerged as part of India's modernist art movement . Singh’s paintings were commonly built around an ambiguous female protagonist, surrounded by fragmented texts, flowers, vehicles, and domestic objects of everyday urban Indian life. Often rendered in thick, layered oil paint across crowded, gravity-less pictorial planes, these paintings were compared by critics to South Asian miniature painting and to maps. “I always paint the things I see and experience every day,” she told curator Hans Ulrich Obrist in an interview for the catalogue of her 2025 Serpentine Galleries survey. “They’re almost the same every day.” In works like My Lollipop City: Gemini Rising (2005), bureaucratic figures stand atop a map of New Delhi annotated with road names and constellations, a corner of the canvas warning, in the artist’s own hand, “THE MAP IS FAULTY DO NOT FOLLOW IT.” Her 1993 painting My Mother , among her best-known, divides the canvas along a diagonal road, with a half-length portrait of her mother facing a crowded field of cars, bicycles, soldiers, and crosses. Singh received the Padma Bhushan, India’s third-highest civilian honor, in 2011, and the Lalit Kala Akademi Fellowship in 2014. Her work is held in the collections of the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi, the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, and the Peabody Essex Museum.She is represented in New Delhi by Vadehra Art Gallery . In 2024, her work appeared alongside that of longtime peers Nilima Sheikh , Nalini Malani , and Madhvi Parekh in “The Imaginary Institution of India: Art 1975–1998” at London’s Barbican Centre. The following year, the Serpentine North presented “Remembering,” a 60-year survey and Singh’s first institutional solo exhibition outside India , co-organized with Obrist, the Serpentine’s artistic director, who called her an inspiration to “five generations of Indian contemporary artists.” Roshini Vadehra, her longtime gallerist, said the growing international attention reflected a broader moment for Indian art, driven by “a blend of historical traditions and contemporary relevance that speaks to global concerns: identity, politics, gender, and social transformation.” Her market saw momentum, too. A 16-panel mural-scale work, The Wish Dream (2001), sold for $2.24 million at a Saffronart auction in 2010, a record at the time for a living Indian woman artist. News of Singh’s death drew tributes across the Indian art world. The curator Uma Nair called her “the high priestess of contemporary Indian art” and “the female M.F. Husain of the female arc,” praising the way she “wove violence and chaos and patriarchal mores all so softly.” The poet Ashok Vajpeyi, managing trustee of the Raza Foundation, wrote that “her art survives her life and would now create a new posthumous life of itself.” Singh is survived by her husband. Their only daughter, the artist Anjum Singh, died of cancer in 2020.

title: This Radical Art Collection Is a Sign of Texas’s Reinvention
summary: In some ways, it was the type of event that happens everywhere in the international art world: a convivial gathering of well-heeled guests, free-flowing drinks, and representatives from major galleries including Lisson , Edel Assanti, and Thaddaeus Ropac . In others, it was unmistakably Texan: hefty picanha steaks sizzled over an open fire, while a honky-tonk band provided the soundtrack. Such was the opening of Ostillo, a new art foundation in Austin that opened in September, where, the following evening, at a lavish dinner, artist and musician Lonnie Holley performed live. Between the caliber of the attendees, the scale of the hospitality, and the art itself, the occasion marked an ambitious new arrival on the Austin art scene. It’s a telling moment for a city that has been transforming for years, and for a state entering a new political chapter after November’s midterms delivered Texas Democrats their first statewide victories since 1994. Austin, long celebrated for its independent music scene and laid-back character, has become a magnet for technology companies, wealth, and new residents. Soho House opened on South Congress Avenue in 2021, while the city’s cultural institutions have grown in size and status. The Blanton Museum of Art unveiled its redesigned grounds in 2023, and the Emma S. Barrientos Mexican American Cultural Center reopened following a major expansion this June. Against this backdrop, Ostillo represents another dimension of Austin’s transformation: a foundation dedicated to showing challenging contemporary art, free of charge. It grew out of the collection of local real estate developer René Campos, who, with the help of Paris-based art advisor and founding director Sacha Zerbib, has spent the last decade assembling more than 90 works. Zerbib and Campos first met in Paris in 2016 through a shared interest in architecture. Although Campos had long been fascinated by history and art, he had yet to begin collecting seriously. “Every time he steps into a new place, the first thing he goes to is a museum,” Zerbib said. “That is the kind of mindset he has: always ready to learn.” Their first acquisition together was something of a test of Campos’s appetite for experimentation: a monumental, 2.5-meter-wide stripe painting by German artist Günther Förg . Hardly an obvious starting point, it established a relationship built on trust and a willingness to venture into unfamiliar territory. “Very early on I understood that he was not going to go for the eye-candy kind of works, the easily accessible, entertaining art,” Zerbib said. “It was more about a certain darkness, a certain seriousness that the art was going to convey.” That sensibility is evident in Ostillo’s inaugural exhibition, “Masquerade,” on view through spring 2027, which brings together works by artists including Glenn Ligon , Sylvia Snowden , Sanya Kantarovsky , Mohammed Sami , Salman Toor , and Christopher Wool . The exhibition takes its name from Ligon’s Masquerade (2006), a work incorporating text from James Baldwin’s essay “Stranger in the Village.” Exploring identity, displacement, and the ways people conceal or reveal themselves, the show reflects a collection concerned with confronting uncomfortable questions about the human experience. For Zerbib, the guiding principle is “radicality,” which he defines as “uncompromising works” that don’t shy away from difficult ideas, many of which are referenced in the foundation’s very location. Ostillo occupies a transformed industrial building in Rosewood, a historically Black neighborhood of East Austin. The city’s 1928 master plan helped institutionalize racial segregation by concentrating services for Black residents in East Austin. More recently, rapid development and rising property values have reshaped the neighborhood, with modern buildings an increasingly common sight amid the historical surroundings. A brand-new contemporary art foundation here adds another layer to this story of change. Zerbib himself draws a connection between the exhibition’s themes of migration and displacement and Texas’s own complicated history, including slavery and forced migration. The parallels were not intentional, he says, but have become increasingly apparent as the collection has taken shape. Ostillo is also seeking to connect with the neighborhood beyond its exhibition walls. Free to visit, it includes a public library and an outdoor performance space that will serve as the permanent home of the East Side Kings Festival, celebrating the area’s musical heritage. Zerbib has been working with other Austin institutions such as the Blanton Museum of Art and The Contemporary Austin to help Ostillo find its place in the city’s cultural landscape. “As soon as they understood the artists that I was intending to show, they immediately took it seriously,” he recalled. According to Zerbib, Campos decided he wanted to present his collection publicly as early as 2018. “We realized that what we had already acquired was too impactful not to be shared with the public,” he said. There is something characteristically Texan about the impulse. Zerbib sees the foundation as an extension of Campos’s generosity: the same instinct that sees him welcome guests to his ranch and enthusiastically show them around the property for opening weekend. “Texas has something about generosity, hospitality, community, and they love sharing everything,” Zerbib said. Some things, it seems, don’t change, no matter what the political climate.

title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Leon Xu
summary: For Leon Xu , a painting begins with a physical sensation, what he calls “brain tingles.” Whenever he feels that, Xu takes a photo to capture the moment. From these snapshots, the New York–based artist transforms ordinary slices of city life—neon signs, bodega flowers, old cars, the view from a window—into hazy, luminous paintings that strike a balance between real memories and imagined ones. “My work is about the distance between experiencing something and trying to remember it after time has gone by,” he explained. “By the time I’m painting it, it’s already three layers removed from the original moment. It’s almost like a more vivid new thing.” This is not a goodbye, 2026 Leon Xu Mai 36 Galerie Send me an Angel, 2026 Leon Xu Mai 36 Galerie Xu grew up painting, with a photographer father who helped shape his eye. In the studio, he keeps his reference photos in his peripheral vision, glancing at them only occasionally, if needed. His technique, airbrush layered with brushwork, reflects his teenage years making graffiti in San Francisco, Born in Zhongshan, China, and raised in San Francisco, Xu moved to New York in 2019. Today, he works from a Chinatown studio, chosen for its proximity to the streets that inspire him. His daily walks in the neighborhood yield subjects ranging from takeout spots to jewelry displays. Muah!, 2026 Leon Xu Mai 36 Galerie Xu’s career took off during the pandemic, when he began painting daily and sharing his work on Instagram. In 2022, he had his first solo exhibition with Zürich’s Mai 36 Galerie , “Wishful Thinking,” followed by “ Afterglow ” in 2025. The gallery announced its representation of Xu in July 2026 and will have presented his work at Art Basel, ARCOmadrid, ACK Kyoto, and Art Basel Miami Beach 2026 this year. A major painting will enter the collection of the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, in December. title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Diambe
summary: For Brazilian artist Diambe , the natural world is both material and subject. They cast bronze from beeswax, paint in egg tempera on linen, and color their sculptures and paintings with mineral pigments derived from stones. “The way that things change in nature and how we’re all subjected to forces that we cannot control properly is something that I try to make evident in my work,” Diambe told us. title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Danielle Fretwell
summary: At first glance, Danielle Fretwell ’s paintings look like lavish feasts. Fish, berries, flowers, silverware, and antique linens are rendered in rich detail, recalling the still lifes of the Dutch Golden Age . Some are alluring arrangements of objects and delicacies, while others depict banquet scenes partially obscured by swaths of abstraction, creating a push and pull between what’s revealed and what’s hidden. “I have an interest in truth and what it takes for someone to trust something or someone,” the New Hampshire–based artist told us. Second Nature, 2026 Danielle Fretwell Alice Amati Set Piece, 2026 Danielle Fretwell Alice Amati In her “split still lifes,” Fretwell meticulously stages and photographs her arrangements before rendering them in oil paint on large canvases. She then adds a layer of thinned paint, pressing sheets and foam into the wet surface to create an abstract veil of color. “I try to create spaces that are a bit difficult for the viewer to enter, hoping that sparks a sense of discomfort,” she explained. Her compositions suggest a sumptuous meal about to begin, one the viewer will never fully witness. Fretwell finds the tableware, candlesticks, and linens in her paintings at antique shops. “I think that I’m really drawn to objects that have a tension between attraction and repulsion,” she told us. “I love the cycle and circulation of objects and how objects long outlive the people who once owned them.” Dissonance, 2026 Danielle Fretwell Alice Amati Fretwell earned her MFA from Boston University in 2021, and the years since have brought a steady run of firsts. She is represented by Alice Amati in London, where she had her first solo exhibition, “ Shallow Invitations ,” in 2024, followed by a solo booth at NADA New York in 2025 and a second solo show with the gallery, “ Tablescapes ,” that fall. This summer, she made her New York solo debut with “ Terms of Consumption ” at Olney Gleason , and Alice Amati recently presented her work at Artissima in Turin. We caught up with Fretwell in New Hampshire, joining her on a hunt for antique candlesticks before heading back to her home studio, where she showed us how she builds her compositions and paints them. title: How to Collect Small Sculpture, According to Experts
summary: Small-scale sculpture has a serious history. In the ancient world, handheld sculptures often served as votive objects or fertility icons, central to both ritual and personal life. During the Renaissance, maquettes—small-scale studies for larger sculptures—became a key step in the development of the era’s artworks. In the 20th century, meanwhile, the likes of Alberto Giacometti ’s evocative figures and Constantin Brâncuși ’s studies and small-scale works helped revolutionize modern sculpture. Collecting tabletop sculpture comes with its own pleasures and peculiarities, factoring in display, scale, and context. These are objects that can live in personal spaces—on coffee tables or bookshelves—and thrive in stand-alone settings. Such nuances and choices are what lend small sculptures their power and complexity. “You don’t just look at a tabletop sculpture from one direction. You walk around it and notice how the light changes its surface, and discover details over time,” said Raimonda Ameti, director at Antwerp gallery Objects With Narratives . The hurdles in buying smaller sculptures are often more psychological than practical. Sotiris Sotiriou, founder of COMA in Sydney, calls the main barrier “confidence rather than price.” Elizabeth Feld, director at Hirschl & Adler , is more to the point. “People are terrified of knocking things over,” she said. Understanding materials For some would-be collectors, understanding material and medium can feel opaque and daunting. It need not be. While small-scale sculpture can be made from a dazzling range of materials, most works can be categorized as one of the following: bronze and cast metal , ceramics , stone , glass , wood , or assemblage —which often mixes different media. In terms of display, these works don’t require too much specialized care, but each has its own unique qualities to consider. Bronze and cast metal sculptures are, for instance, among the oldest sculptural materials, dating back to the ancient world. Artists and collectors continue to embrace them today. “With bronze, you want to understand the casting and patina,” said Ameti. Asking the seller whether the artist or a specialist foundry made the piece is a smart ask, she notes. One of the hottest collecting categories today, ceramic and clay range from hand-built one-offs to kiln-fired editions. The unique and unpredictable qualities of fired works are what often appeal; a kind of magic transformation takes place in the kiln. The experts Artsy spoke to advise collectors to examine the glaze, the surface, and how the piece was fired. “We’ve seen considerable interest in ceramics and works that foreground their material qualities,” said Sotiriou. “I think part of this comes from an increasing appreciation for process and craft. Collectors are interested in understanding how something was made, whether that’s the unpredictability of a ceramic firing, the physicality of carving stone, or the transformation involved in casting bronze.” While stone sculptures are rarer at a tabletop scale, they’re worth seeking out, as marble and alabaster have a weight and permanence other materials lack. For these materials, which can be fragile, ask the gallery about handling and care. Off To See The Wizard, 2025 Hedy Yang Galerie Robertson Arès Neighborling Maquette 25, 2025 Seth Clark Paradigm Gallery + Studio For a more affordable entry point, resin and glass can be accessible. Quality can vary widely, however, so check clarity and surface finish, and whether any edition is properly documented. Found and assembled objects are a distinct tradition in which meaning is often inseparable from the materials, so ask the seller or artist what was used and why. “We always encourage people to ask questions about how a work was made,” said Ameti. But don’t hold out for perfection. Irregularities and marks can be what make a work special, as long as they are intentional. Ameti sees growing interest in ceramics, bronze, and stone, driven by buyers who want to see the maker’s hand, with its texture, imperfections, and process. Sotiriou offers a useful test for any of them: is the material necessary to the work, and is the artist doing something compelling with it? How to live with small sculpture Untitled, 2026 Yuji Ueda COMA Unlike a framed work, which arrives with its own border, tabletop sculpture depends heavily on its setting. The galleries we spoke to advised starting with scale. A work that is too small vanishes on a large console, and one that is too large crowds it. A general rule is that a sculpture should occupy a third to half the depth of the surface, meaning a shelf that’s 12-inches deep could be home to a work with a 6-inch footprint, whereas a 36-inch coffee table might look best with a sculpture measuring about a foot wide. Of course, the ultimate aesthetic test for what looks right is the collector’s eye. “A small sculpture doesn’t necessarily require much physical space, but it does benefit from visual space,” said Sotiriou. Ameti agrees, saying not to overcrowd an environment: “A small sculpture doesn’t need much room, but it does need a bit of breathing space. You don’t want it to disappear between too many other objects.” A good rule of thumb is to choose a spot that offers several angles, such as a shelf or console you pass daily, without over-optimizing for one view. Feld recalls advising a client on a pair of entry-hall niches, where the planned built-in wooden pedestals pulled attention away from the works and left the space feeling cold and stilted. “Once we removed the bases and selected sculptures that were freestanding, the space became welcoming, warm, and interactive,” she said. Ameti tells collectors to remember they are living in a home. “We also don’t believe sculpture should always be displayed on a pedestal or treated like something in a museum,” she said. Torso, about 1988 Elizabeth Catlett Hirschl & Adler Fragment 1, 2021 Maria Elena González Hirschl & Adler Light matters just as much. “A work of art can either come alive or get totally overlooked by the right or the wrong—or a lack of—lighting,” said Feld. Light exposure from the side reveals texture in ceramic and bronze, while direct overhead light can flatten a work, so try moving a small lamp until it lights the piece from slightly to the side. Check it in daylight and in evening light too. With children or pets at home, look for a bookshelf or niche where a work is unlikely to be knocked over. Finally, consider whether to show a piece alone or in a group. A single strong work can read better alone, and groupings work when something connects them, such as material, scale, palette, or maker. Feld has seen “more is more” rooms succeed when every object is special, but avoid a shelf of unrelated things competing for attention. Assessing value Angel I, 2023 Conrad Hicks Objects With Narratives Sakura TFO26002, 2026 Maarten Vrolijk Objects With Narratives No matter the material that a sculpture is made of, one should always buy the best quality work of art they can afford at a given moment,” Feld said. “Not only will this guarantee survival over time, but it will help to maintain the value of what they have invested in a work.” Like all media, prices for tabletop sculptures can vary widely. Under $500, the experts say to look for ceramic and resin by emerging makers, or open editions by established artists. From $500 to $2,500—the most active range for serious collectors—you’ll find original ceramics, small bronze editions, and cast works by gallery-represented artists. From $2,500 to $10,000, expect signed, numbered editions in bronze or ceramic by established names and unique hand-built works by represented artists. Above that, you’re looking at unique or rare editions by established artists that can veer into blue-chip names such as Giacometti et al. Sotiriou suggests asking a gallery whether the piece represents something essential about that practice. Ameti notes that value shouldn’t be defined by price alone. “We look at the quality of the work, the artist’s approach, and whether there’s something about the object that stays with you,” she said. “We always prefer someone to buy one piece they genuinely love rather than several pieces simply because they seem like a good deal.” Seed Deposit (II), 2026 Anna May Kirk COMA Edition status matters more at this scale than for most other media. An edition is a fixed number of near-identical copies cast from one original, with the total set in advance by the artist. Open editions have no limit to the number produced, which is why they often cost less. A bronze in an edition of three is a meaningfully different object from the same cast in an edition of 500. Ask how many were made, whether artist’s proofs or variations exist, whether the work is unique, and who fabricated it. Most handmade work is unique, however. “Clients should always ask if a sculpture is a multiple, but they will find that most handmade works of art are unique as it is impossible to replicate something handmade so precisely,” Feld said. Still, the first rule of art buying remains: purchase what you love. “For us, collecting should start with a genuine connection to the work. Everything else, including edition size, comes after that,” Ameti summed up.

title: The 2027 Met Gala theme is “extraORDINARY,” highlighting the beauty of the everyday.
summary: The Metropolitan Museum of Art has announced “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” as the Costume Institute's spring 2027 exhibition. The exhibition will be on view May 9, 2027, through January 9, 2028, at the Met Fifth Avenue. The accompanying Met Gala fundraiser will take place Monday, May 3, 2027. This theme replaces the previous, now-canceled exhibition “ John Galliano : Horizons,” a planned retrospective that would have made Galliano the third living designer honored by the Costume Institute. The Met and Galliano jointly called off that show on August 31st, after weeks of criticism over Galliano's 2011 antisemitic and racist remarks, which had gotten him fined and fired from Dior. “extraORDINARY,” with its deliberately modest theme of jeans, T-shirts, and everyday materials, is a conspicuously low-key follow-up to a controversy that had centered on Galliano’s penchant for excesses. Drawing on the Costume Institute's collection alongside loans and new acquisitions, the show examines how designers rework familiar garments and ordinary materials— such as jeans, T-shirts, puffer coats, paper, plastic, metal—through craft, construction, and conceptual wit, while their earlier functions and histories remain embedded in what the new designs mean. “Fashion offers an immediate and compelling way to look at the world,” said Max Hollein, director and CEO of the museum. “By bringing together works that begin with the clothes, objects, and materials of daily life, extraORDINARY invites visitors to discover the creativity and ingenuity in things they encounter every day.” Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute's curator in charge, framed the show as a meditation on familiarity itself. “A pair of jeans, a white shirt, or a sweatshirt can hold traces of a life—the habits, memories, and attachments that make something our own. Designers work with that familiarity, revealing unexpected possibilities within forms and materials we think we already know," he said. Bolton has also described the show as a follow-up to this year's “Costume Art,” telling the New York Times that "each focuses on how clothes are worn." The exhibition, expected to bring together some 200 to 230 pieces including loans and pieces from the Costume Institute's archive, opens with garments from Jun Takahashi 's fall/winter 2024–25 Undercover collection “Watching a Working Woman,” inspired partly by Wim Wenders 's 2023 film Perfect Days . Two central sections follow. The first, “Familiar Forms,” groups archetypal garments—puffer coats, jeans, flannel shirts, and biker jackets—to trace how shifts in scale and material unsettle their recognizability. The second, “Common Matter,” is organized around paper, plastic, and metal, featuring works including a 1992 Rei Kawakubo dress for Comme des Garçons and a Helmut Lang jacket. The show closes with selections from Kunihiko Morinaga's Anrealage collections spanning 2009 to 2021, in which garments built around cubes, spheres, and pyramids probe how clothing accommodates—or fails to accommodate—the human body. The exhibition is made possible by Instagram, with major funding from Moncler and additional support from Condé Nast. The Met has not yet announced a dress code for the May 3rd benefit event, but Bolton has suggested it will follow the exhibition's understated register, a departure from the gala's more flamboyant past themes.

title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Mmangaliso Nzuza
summary: Mmangaliso Nzuza wants his paintings to give off the feeling of home. One canvas in his Cape Town studio, As the Red-eyed Dove Sings (2025), takes its title from a bird whose song he remembers hearing as a child. “I wanted to almost capture that memory that it held for me,” he told us. “I want them to feel like what I feel when I think about home.” His paintings, which primarily depict human figures, are built from bold, angular forms that nod to Cubism . Nzuza became interested in how Picasso , Braque , and other Cubists drew on African masks and sculptural traditions. “This has almost been a way of reclaiming that into my culture,” he reflected. Held Voices, 2026 Mmangaliso Nzuza Southern Guild Assembly, 2026 Mmangaliso Nzuza Southern Guild During breaks from painting, he takes long walks, gathering impressions of his surroundings before returning to his studio in Woodstock, where Table Mountain rises in the distance. There, he prefers to dive straight into painting rather than plan his compositions. “Going straight onto the canvas allows my innermost emotions to flow,” he explained. Nzuza’s rise has been swift. He began painting in earnest during the pandemic in 2020, when his mother bought him paints and encouraged his artistic inclinations. He started sharing his work on Instagram, and it quickly drew attention. He later connected with Southern Guild , which presented his first solo exhibition in Cape Town in 2024. Hymn in Iridescence, 2025 Mmangaliso Nzuza Southern Guild In April 2026, his exhibition “Ballad of the Peacock” helped inaugurate the gallery’s new Tribeca space and marked his U.S. solo debut. His work has since appeared at Frieze London and The Armory Show and entered the collections of the North Dakota Museum of Art and the Montecito Contemporary Art Collection. He’ll also be featured at Art Basel Miami Beach in December. We caught up with Nzuza in his studio, where he shared his work, process, and inspirations. “I would describe my work as something that invokes a feeling, a memory,” he said. “Most importantly, I want it to feel familiar.” Watch the video above and explore The Artsy Vanguard 2027 .
